newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia seen facing live cattle export boom.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia seen facing live cattle export boom.

text.p: Australian live cattle exports are likely to continue to grow strongly, the New South Wales Farmers' Association was told on Thursday.
Rick Wright, chairman of the association's cattle committee, said exports were likely to exceed 750,000 head in 1996/97 to June 30, an increase of 500 percent or 520,000 since 1988.

This would compare with 633,000 head of live cattle exports in 1995/96, he said. Responding to a question about whether live cattle were about to be "processed" during shipping to avoid Australian industrial relations problems, Wright said that this was "probably a fair way out".
Australian cattle are increasingly being processed in the Philippines and Indonesia where costs were one-tenth of processing in Australia.
New Zealand and Argentina are beating Australia in the costs of processing, he said. But the alternative of slaughter on the water was "not silly," he said.
The association passed a resolution to press for the development of a live cattle export port in the state of New South Wales.
Most Australian live cattle are now exported from Darwin, in Australia's far north.

Asked whether Argentina posed a threat to Australian beef exports on the world market, Wright said the country did not presently have sufficient infrastructure, although it would solve this problem in five years time.
"It's not an immediate threat but it will be in five years," he said. "We are 10,000 km closer to the Asian market-if we can't beat them over 10,000 km we should give it away."

Wright said that the beyond its present crisis, the Australian beef industry was seeing new markets evolve, domestic and international consumption of fast food increase, and problems in white meat beginning to arise.
Australia also had a distinct geographical advantage in proximity to the fastest growing economies in the world in Asia, he said. Prospects in Asia were exciting, he said.
In Asia, the new generation of people consumed large quantities of meat products, and prospects were good, he said.
Wright also said that the Australian drive to emphasise mince products was finding success and could open new channels for sales to Asia.
It raised the prospect of Australia exporting as mince beef products which otherwise would not be finished, he said.
